mainTopic: The drizzle and the growing scholar; a scholar's temper; improper requests answered by ה׳; who taught when we ask for rain
overview: The amud opens by finishing the גמרא's list of kinds of rain with the gentle drizzle, which helps even a seed buried under a clod of earth. רבא uses that image for a young Torah scholar: once he starts to grow, he keeps growing. Sayings follow about the 'fire' and 'iron' of a תלמיד חכם, and רבינא balances them: a person must still train himself to be gentle. Next, רבי יונתן lists three people who made risky requests. אליעזר and שאול were answered well, but יפתח was answered badly, and two פסוקים in ירמיהו are read as hints to his story. רבי ברכיה adds that כנסת ישראל also asked improperly, comparing ה׳ to rain and to a seal, and ה׳ answered with something better and constant: dew, and engraving Israel on His palms. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה and asks whose opinion says we ask for rain only near the rainy season. רבא says רבי יהושע, and אביי says it could even be רבי אליעזר, since asking and mentioning are separate. A second version of this discussion begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Drizzle helps even a buried seed
steps.stepSummary: The gentle drizzle (עוּרְפִּילָא) is good even for a seed lying under a clod of earth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Drizzle is beneficial even to a seed under a clod of earth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its list of different kinds of rain by praising the light drizzle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heavy rain can damage things, but a fine drizzle seeps gently everywhere. It even reaches a seed hidden under a lump of earth and helps it grow. This image is the setup for רבא's comparison in step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: A clod or lump of earth

phrases.english: Drizzle —
even to a seed under a clod of earth
is beneficial to it.

steps.triggerLanguage: עוּרְפִּילָא אֲפִילּוּ לְפַרְצִידָא דְּתוּתֵי קָלָא מַהְנְיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the previous section's discussion of the kinds of rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Drizzle benefits even a seed buried under a clod.

steps.title: What does the word for drizzle mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where the word עוּרְפִּילָא comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is 'urpila'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask what the unusual word for drizzle means. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is about the word itself, not about any law. The גמרא wants to show that the name hints at what drizzle does.

phrases.english: What is 'urpila'?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי עוּרְפִּילָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the meaning of the word used in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning and origin of the word עוּרְפִּילָא.

steps.title: Drizzle means 'Arise, furrows'
steps.stepSummary: עוּרְפִּילָא is read as עוּרוּ פִּילֵי, 'Arise, furrows'.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means 'Arise, furrows.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word is a blend of two words meaning 'wake up, furrows'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The drizzle is pictured as calling to the furrows in the field to wake up and produce. This fits step 1: drizzle gets the buried seeds going.

phrases.english: Arise, furrows.
phrases.notes: A word play: עורפילא sounds like עורו פילי.

steps.triggerLanguage: עוּרוּ פִּילֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: עוּרְפִּילָא = עוּרוּ פִּילֵי, the rain that wakes up the furrows.

steps.title: A young scholar is like a buried seed
steps.stepSummary: רבא compares a young Torah scholar to a seed under a clod: once he sprouts, he keeps on sprouting.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A young Torah scholar is like a seed under a clod of earth. Once he sprouts, he keeps sprouting.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא borrows the seed image from step 1 and uses it for a young Torah scholar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A seed under a clod may look stuck at first. But once it breaks through, it keeps growing. In the same way, a young scholar may seem slow at first, but once he starts to grow in Torah, his greatness keeps increasing.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
This young Torah scholar
is like a seed under a clod of earth,
for once he sprouts, he keeps sprouting.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא הַאי צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן דָּמֵי לְפַרְצִידָא דְּתוּתֵי קָלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the seed image from step 1 for a new teaching about Torah scholars.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A young scholar, once he begins to grow, keeps on growing.

steps.title: A scholar's anger comes from his Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that when a Torah scholar boils with anger, it is the Torah inside him that heats him up, since Torah is like fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: When a Torah scholar gets heated, it is the Torah that heats him up, as it says, 'Is not My word like fire, says ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: Since the topic is now Torah scholars, the גמרא brings another saying of רבא, this time about a scholar's temper.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא says a scholar's anger should be understood kindly: the fire of Torah burns inside him. He backs this with the פסוק that compares ה׳'s word to fire.

keyTerms.meaning: Makes him boil, heats him up

phrases.english: And Rava said:
This Torah scholar who boils with anger,
it is the Torah that makes him boil,
as it is stated:
'Is not My word like fire, says ה׳.'
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 23:29

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא הַאי צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן דְּרָתַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another saying of רבא about Torah scholars, now about their temper.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A scholar's anger is caused by the fire of Torah within him.

steps.title: A real scholar is hard as iron
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says a Torah scholar who is not firm like iron is not a true תלמיד חכם, based on the second half of the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Any Torah scholar who is not hard as iron is not a Torah scholar, as it says, 'And like a hammer that shatters rock.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי adds to the same idea: a true scholar must be firm and strong, not weak and wavering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא used the 'fire' part of the פסוק. רב אשי uses the 'hammer' part, which shows Torah is strong and breaks through. So a real scholar must be firm like iron.

phrases.english: And Rav Ashi said:
Any Torah scholar
who is not hard as iron
is not a Torah scholar,
as it is stated: 'And like a hammer that shatters rock.'
phrases.notes: Same פסוק as before, ירמיהו 23:29.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי כׇּל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁאֵינוֹ קָשֶׁה כַּבַּרְזֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the same פסוק as step 5, using its second half.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A true scholar must be firm like iron.

steps.title: A different source: the land whose builders are iron
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא tells רב אשי that they learn the same idea from a different פסוק: 'a land whose stones are iron', read as 'whose builders are iron'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said to רב אשי: You learn it from there. We learn it from here, as it is written, 'A land whose stones are iron.' Do not read 'its stones' but 'its builders.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא agrees with רב אשי's idea but gives a different פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads אֲבָנֶיהָ ('its stones') as בּוֹנֶיהָ ('its builders'). The builders of the land are its Torah scholars, so the פסוק says they are 'iron'. The point stays the same; only the source changes.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not read (a reading that changes the vowels to bring out a hidden meaning)

steps.confusionAlert: רבי אבא is not arguing with רב אשי's idea. He agrees with the idea and just learns it from a different פסוק.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said to Rav Ashi:
You learn it from there.
We learn it from here,
as it is written: 'A land whose stones are iron.'
phrases.notes: דברים 8:9

phrases.english: Do not read 'its stones,'
but rather 'its builders.'
phrases.notes: The 'builders' are the Torah scholars, so they are the ones called 'iron'.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתּוּן מֵהָתָם מַתְנִיתוּ לַהּ אֲנַן מֵהָכָא מַתְנֵינַן לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different פסוק as the source for רב אשי's idea.
steps.raayaObject: That a Torah scholar must be hard as iron.

steps.title: Even so, train yourself to be gentle
steps.stepSummary: רבינא balances the praise of toughness: a person must still teach himself to act gently, as the פסוק says, 'Remove anger from your heart.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Even so, a person needs to teach himself to be gentle, as it says, 'Remove anger from your heart.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא puts a limit on everything just said about fire and iron: a scholar still has to work on being calm and gentle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 5 to 7 could make it sound as if anger and harshness are fine for a scholar. רבינא says no: even though Torah may make him firm, he must train himself to act gently and remove anger from his heart.
steps.whatToRemember: A תלמיד חכם may burn with the fire of Torah and be firm as iron, but he must still train himself to act gently and keep anger out of his heart.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the right balance for how a Torah scholar should behave: firmness in Torah, but gentleness in how he acts.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Even so,
a person needs
to teach himself to act gently,
as it is stated: 'And remove anger from your heart, etc.'
phrases.notes: קהלת 11:10

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא אֲפִילּוּ הָכִי מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְאִינִישׁ לְמֵילַף נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּנִיחוּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the praise of a scholar's fire and toughness in steps 5 to 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a scholar must train himself to act gently and remove anger.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Firmness in Torah, but gentleness in how one acts.

steps.title: Three who asked improperly
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן teaches that three people asked improperly; two got a good answer and one got a bad answer: אליעזר, שאול, and יפתח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: Three asked improperly. Two were answered properly, and one was answered improperly. They are: אליעזר, אברהם's servant; שאול בן קיש; and יפתח from גלעד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic: a list of three people who made risky requests. This sets up the explanation of each case that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of the three made a request that could have turned out badly. Two were saved and got a good outcome, while one got the bad outcome his request allowed. The details of each come next.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
Three asked improperly,
phrases.notes: He means their requests were risky and could have turned out badly.

phrases.english: two were answered properly,
one was answered improperly.
And these are they:
Eliezer, the servant of Abraham,
and Saul son of Kish,
and Jephthah the Gileadite.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן שְׁלֹשָׁה שָׁאֲלוּ שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the scholar sayings before it. It lays the groundwork for רבי ברכיה's 'also' (אַף) statement about rain in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three made improper requests: two were answered favorably and one unfavorably.

steps.title: Eliezer's open-ended sign at the well
steps.stepSummary: אליעזר set a sign that any girl who offered water would be the wife for יצחק. She could have been lame or blind, but ה׳ answered properly and sent רבקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליעזר, the servant of אברהם, said: 'The girl to whom I say, please lower your jug...' (she will be the one). That girl could even have been lame or blind. ה׳ answered him properly, and רבקה came his way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first name on רבי יונתן's list, אליעזר, and shows why his request was improper.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אליעזר's sign only tested whether the girl was kind. It said nothing about whether she was fit in other ways, so a girl with a serious defect could have passed it. Even so, ה׳ sent him the perfect match, רבקה.

keyTerms.meaning: It could have been (here: his words left room for this)
He answered him properly (a good outcome)
Came his way, happened to meet him

phrases.english: Eliezer, the servant of Abraham —
as it is written: 'And it shall be that the maiden'
to whom I shall say,
'Please lower your jug, etc.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 24:14

phrases.english: It could have been even a lame girl, even a blind one.
He answered him properly,
phrases.notes: The one answering is ה׳. The גמרא doesn't say it outright.

phrases.english: and Rebecca came his way.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֱלִיעֶזֶר עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the first of the three cases listed by רבי יונתן in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אליעזר's sign allowed for an unfit bride, yet ה׳ answered properly with רבקה.

steps.title: Shaul's open-ended reward for killing Goliath
steps.stepSummary: שאול promised his daughter to whoever killed גלית. That man could have been a slave or a ממזר, but ה׳ answered properly and it was דוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: שאול בן קיש said: 'The man who kills him, the king will make him very rich and give him his daughter.' That man could even have been a slave or a ממזר‎. ה׳ answered him properly, and דוד came his way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second name on the list, שאול, using the same pattern as אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שאול's offer was open to anyone, including people who could not marry the king's daughter at all. The danger was real, but ה׳ sent דוד, a fitting husband.

keyTerms.meaning: A child born from a forbidden union, who may not marry a regular Jewish woman

phrases.english: Saul son of Kish —
as it is written: 'And it shall be that the man who strikes him down,'
the king will enrich him with great wealth
and will give him his daughter.'
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:25

phrases.english: It could have been even a slave, even a mamzer.
He answered him properly,
and David came his way.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאוּל בֶּן קִישׁ דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second case in the same pattern as step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שאול's offer allowed for an unfit winner, yet ה׳ answered properly with דוד.

steps.title: Yiftach's open-ended vow and its tragic answer
steps.stepSummary: יפתח vowed to offer as a קרבן whatever came out of his house first. It could have been a non-kosher animal. This time ה׳ answered improperly, and his daughter came out.
steps.simpleTranslation: יפתח from גלעד said: 'Whatever comes out of the doors of my house (I will offer as a קרבן).' It could even have been something impure. ה׳ answered him improperly, and his daughter came his way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third name, יפתח, the one who received a bad answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the first two, יפתח's words left room for a bad result: a non-kosher animal cannot be a קרבן. Unlike them, he was not saved from his careless words. His daughter came out first.

keyTerms.meaning: Something impure, such as a non-kosher animal

steps.confusionAlert: Both 'proper' and 'improper' describe ה׳'s answer, not the request. All three requests were improper. The difference is only in how each one turned out.

phrases.english: Jephthah the Gileadite —
as it is written: 'And it shall be that whatever comes out,'
that comes out of the doors of my house, etc.'
phrases.notes: שופטים 11:31. He vowed to offer it as a קרבן.

phrases.english: It could have been even something impure.
He answered him improperly:
his daughter came his way.

steps.triggerLanguage: יִפְתַּח הַגִּלְעָדִי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third case, which breaks the pattern of a good outcome.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יפתח's vow allowed for an impure animal, and ה׳ answered improperly: his daughter came out.

steps.title: The prophet's hint: was there no healer in Gilad?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ties יפתח's story to a פסוק in which the נביא asks whether there is no balm or healer in גלעד.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what the נביא said to the Jewish people: 'Is there no balm in גלעד? Is there no healer there?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק that it reads as a hint to יפתח's story. The next step adds a second פסוק about יפתח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יפתח came from גלעד, and the פסוק asks why no cure was found there. The common explanation is that a way out of the terrible vow existed, because the vow could have been released, but no one used it.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what (the פסוק) means when it says

steps.whatToRemember: All three people asked carelessly. אליעזר and שאול were saved by a good answer, while יפתח suffered a bad one, and the נביא hints that even then a cure was available.

phrases.english: And this is what the prophet said to Israel:
'Is there no balm in Gilead?
Is there no healer there?'
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 8:22. יפתח was from גלעד, which is why this פסוק fits.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּקָאָמַר לְהוּ נָבִיא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attaches a פסוק to the יפתח case from step 12 as a hint to it.
steps.raayaObject: The tragedy of יפתח's vow and the cure that went unused
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיהו 8:22, 'Is there no balm in גלעד?'

steps.title: A second פסוק showing ה׳ never wanted יפתח's sacrifice
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a פסוק from ירמיהו and reads its three phrases as three people: the son of מישע, יפתח, and יצחק.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'Which I did not command, and I did not speak, nor did it come into My heart.' 'Which I did not command' is the son of מישע king of מואב, as it says: 'He took his firstborn son, who would reign after him, and offered him as a burnt offering.' 'And I did not speak' is יפתח. 'Nor did it come into My heart' is יצחק son of אברהם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another פסוק to show that יפתח's sacrifice of his daughter was something ה׳ never wanted. It splits the פסוק into three phrases and gives each one a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 used the גלעד פסוק to show יפתח's story went badly. Now the phrase 'I did not speak' is read as being about יפתח, so ה׳ never told him to offer his daughter. The פסוק also covers two other cases: מישע, which ה׳ never commanded, and יצחק, which ה׳ never truly intended.

keyTerms.meaning: מישע, king of מואב, who offered his own son as a sacrifice
It did not come into My heart, meaning I never intended it

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is saying ה׳ never told אברהם to bring יצחק‎. ה׳ did command it. The point is that ה׳ never meant for יצחק to actually be killed.

phrases.english: And it is written: "Which I did not command,
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 19:5. The פסוק is about people burning their children as offerings.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא דִבַּרְתִּי וְלֹא עָלְתָה עַל לִבִּי״,
phrases.english: and I did not speak, nor did it come into My heart."

phrases.aramaic: ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא צִוֵּיתִי״ — זֶה בְּנוֹ שֶׁל מֵישַׁע מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב,
phrases.english: "Which I did not command": this is the son of Mesha, king of Moab,
as it is said: "He took his firstborn son
who would reign after him, and offered him up as a burnt offering."
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 3:27

phrases.english: "And I did not speak": this is Jephthah.

phrases.aramaic: ״וְלֹא עָלְתָה עַל לִבִּי״ — זֶה יִצְחָק בֶּן אַבְרָהָם.
phrases.english: "Nor did it come into My heart": this is Isaac son of Abraham.
phrases.notes: ה׳ did tell אברהם to bring יצחק, but He never meant for it to really happen.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְתִיב: ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא צִוִּיתִי וְלֹא דִבַּרְתִּי וְלֹא עָלְתָה עַל לִבִּי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second פסוק to support step 13's point that יפתח was answered improperly.
steps.raayaObject: That יפתח's offering of his daughter was never wanted by ה׳
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיהו 19:5, with 'ולא דברתי' read as being about יפתח

steps.title: כנסת ישראל also asked improperly by comparing ה׳ to rain
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברכיה says the Jewish people also asked in an improper way, yet ה׳ answered properly. The proof is a פסוק in הושע that compares ה׳'s coming to rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ברכיה said: כנסת ישראל also asked improperly, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, answered it properly, as it says: 'Let us know, let us strive to know ה׳. His going forth is sure as the dawn, and He will come to us like the rain.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברכיה adds one more example to the list of people who asked improperly. This time it is the whole Jewish people. His statement sets up ה׳'s answer, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'also' ties this to רבי יונתן's list in step 9. The improper part is in the פסוק's wording: they asked ה׳ to come to them 'like rain.' The step tells us ה׳ answered properly but does not yet explain how. That is explained next, and it brings the גמרא back to its main topic of rain.

keyTerms.meaning: The community of Israel, the Jewish people as a whole
Improperly, in a way that is not fitting

phrases.english: Rabbi Berekhya said:

phrases.aramaic: אַף כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁאֲלָה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן,
phrases.english: The Congregation of Israel also asked improperly,
and the Holy One, Blessed be He, answered her properly,
as it is said: "Let us know, let us strive to know the Lord;
His going forth is sure as the dawn,
and He will come to us like the rain."
phrases.notes: הושע 6:3

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי בֶּרֶכְיָה: אַף כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁאֲלָה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fourth case to רבי יונתן's list of improper requests and turns toward the topic of rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כנסת ישראל asked improperly by comparing ה׳ to rain, yet ה׳ answered properly.

steps.title: ה׳ promises to be like dew, which is always wanted
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ explains that rain is only sometimes wanted, so He will instead be like dew, which is always wanted.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to her: My daughter, you are asking for something that is sometimes wanted and sometimes not wanted. But I will be for you something that is always wanted, as it says: 'I will be like the dew to Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: ה׳ explains what was improper about the request and gives His better answer. This completes the rain example; a second example of the same pattern follows in steps 17-18.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The flaw was that rain is not always a blessing; sometimes people don't want it. ה׳'s 'proper' answer swaps rain for dew, which is always welcome. So He gives a better comparison than the one they asked for, proven from another פסוק in הושע.

keyTerms.meaning: My daughter, a loving way ה׳ addresses the Jewish people

steps.whatToRemember: Four improper requests: אליעזר, שאול, and כנסת ישראל were answered properly, while יפתח was answered badly. Israel asked for ה׳ to come 'like rain,' which is sometimes unwanted. ה׳ promised to be 'like dew,' which is always a blessing.
steps.whyThisMatters: This links the aggadah back to the מסכת's main subject of rain and dew. It shows that dew has a special status as a blessing that is always wanted.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to her:
My daughter, you are asking for something
that is sometimes wanted and sometimes not wanted,
phrases.notes: He means rain: it's a blessing at some times, but not at every time.

phrases.english: but I will be for you
something that is always wanted,
as it is said: "I will be like the dew to Israel."
phrases.notes: הושע 14:6

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: בִּתִּי, אַתְּ שׁוֹאֶלֶת דָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how ה׳ answered properly the improper request from step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ will be like dew, which is always wanted, rather than rain, which is only sometimes wanted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even when Israel asks improperly, ה׳ answers properly by giving a constant blessing, like dew.

steps.title: Israel asks to be a seal on ה׳'s heart and arm
steps.stepSummary: The Jewish people made another improper request. They asked ה׳ to set them like a seal on His heart and on His arm.
steps.simpleTranslation: And she (the Jewish people) also asked in an improper way. She said before Him: Master of the World! 'Set me as a seal on Your heart, as a seal on Your arm.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more example of the Jewish people asking ה׳ in a way that was not quite right. This step gives only the request; ה׳'s answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues רבי ברכיה's theme from steps 15-16, where Israel asked improperly and ה׳ answered properly. The request here comes from a פסוק in שיר השירים. It asks ה׳ to keep Israel close to Him like a seal, a sign worn on the body.

keyTerms.meaning: In an improper or unfitting way
Master of the World, a way of addressing ה׳
A seal, a mark of closeness and belonging

phrases.english: And she also asked in an improper way,
phrases.notes: 'She' is the Jewish people. The גמרא pictures them as a woman speaking to ה׳.

phrases.english: she said before Him: Master of the World!
"Set me as a seal upon Your heart,
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 8:6

phrases.english: as a seal upon Your arm."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹד שָׁאֲלָה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second example of Israel's improper request, parallel to the rain request in steps 15-16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Israel asked to be like a seal on ה׳'s heart and arm.

steps.title: ה׳ engraves Israel on His palms instead
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ says a seal on the heart or arm is only sometimes seen. Instead He will engrave Israel on His palms, which are always seen.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to her: My daughter, you are asking for something that is sometimes seen and sometimes not seen. But I will make for you something that is always seen, as it says: 'Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of My hands.'
steps.whatsHappening: ה׳ answers the request from step 17 with something better. This is the same pattern as the dew-and-rain answer in step 16.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A seal on the heart or arm can be covered by clothing, so it is not always visible. The palms of the hands are always out in the open. ה׳ gives Israel a closeness that never disappears from view.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He

steps.whatToRemember: In both examples (rain and the seal), Israel asked for something that is only sometimes good or seen. ה׳ answered with something that is always there: dew, and engraving on His palms.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to her:
My daughter, you are asking for a thing
that is sometimes seen and sometimes not seen,
but I will make for you
a thing that is always seen,
as it is said: "Behold, I have engraved you on the palms."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 49:16

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives ה׳'s better answer to the request in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ will engrave Israel on His palms, which are always visible, rather than on the heart or arm.

steps.title: Who taught that we ask for rain only near the rainy season?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה. It assumes asking for rain and mentioning rain are the same thing, and asks which תנא the משנה follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'We ask for rain only…' (the משנה). They assumed: asking and mentioning are one thing. Who is the תנא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the stories behind and goes back to the משנה's rule that we ask for rain only close to the rainy season. It asks whose opinion that rule follows, which sets up the answers in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the משנה, רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע argue about when we begin mentioning rain. If asking and mentioning are the same thing, this line of the משנה must match only one of them. So the גמרא wants to know which one.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is the תנא (which sage taught this)?

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two. שאלה is asking 'give dew and rain' (ותן טל ומטר). הזכרה is praising ה׳ as the One who brings rain (משיב הרוח ומוריד הגשם).

phrases.english: "We do not ask for rain…" (and so on).
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. The rest of the line says: only close to the rainy season.

phrases.english: They assumed: asking and mentioning
are one thing,
who is the תנא?

steps.triggerLanguage: סַבְרוּהָ: שְׁאֵלָה וְהַזְכָּרָה חֲדָא מִילְּתָא הִיא, מַאן תַּנָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אגדה and returns to the משנה's halacha.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that we begin asking for rain only near the rainy season, assuming asking and mentioning start at the same time?

steps.title: רבא says it follows רבי יהושע
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the משנה follows רבי יהושע, who says we begin mentioning rain when the לולב is put down.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is רבי יהושע, who said: from the time it is put down.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question from step 19. He matches the משנה to רבי יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע starts mentioning rain on the last day of the festival, after the לולב is no longer taken. That is right before the rainy season. So it fits a משנה that says asking also starts near the rainy season.

phrases.english: רבא said: It is רבי יהושע,
who said: from the time of its putting down.
phrases.notes: 'It' is the לולב. Once we stop taking it, on שמיני עצרת, we start mentioning rain.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה follows רבי יהושע, who begins mentioning rain when the לולב is put down.

steps.title: אביי says it could even follow רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the משנה could even follow רבי אליעזר, because asking and mentioning are two separate things.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: You could even say it is רבי אליעזר. Asking is one thing, and mentioning is another thing.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes back on רבא's answer. He rejects the assumption from step 19 that asking and mentioning are the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר starts mentioning rain on the first day of the festival. אביי says that is only about mentioning. Asking can still begin later, near the rainy season, so the משנה fits רבי אליעזר too.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key idea for the rest of the sugya: asking for rain and mentioning rain can start at different times.

phrases.english: אביי said to him:
You could even say it is רבי אליעזר —
phrases.notes: In the משנה, רבי אליעזר starts mentioning rain on the first day of the festival, earlier than רבי יהושע.

phrases.english: asking is separate, and mentioning is separate.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer by rejecting the starting assumption of step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the משנה must follow only רבי יהושע.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The assumption that asking and mentioning are one thing is wrong. They are separate, so רבי אליעזר can also fit the משנה.

steps.title: A second version of the discussion begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a different version of how this discussion went, opening with 'Let us say.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: Let us say…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a second version of the רבא and אביי discussion. The words 'let us say' open a suggestion that continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Some say' means there was another tradition of how this exchange went. 'Let us say' usually brings a suggestion that the גמרא will test. The full suggestion has not appeared yet.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say, introducing a suggestion

phrases.english: And some say: Let us say

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי: לֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a second version of the discussion in steps 19-21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A suggestion about which תנא the משנה follows. It continues past this point in the text.
